definition: A structured method for improving how work is done. It combines Lean (removing waste and delay) with Six Sigma (reducing variation and defects), and follows the DMAIC phases.
A repeatable sequence of steps that turns inputs (information, materials, requests) into an output someone uses.
Any output that fails a customer requirement. A single unit can have several defects. Compare defective: a unit with at least one defect.
The fact that repeated outputs of a process are not identical. Measured with the range or the standard deviation. Six Sigma exists to understand and reduce it.
A data-driven method for reducing variation and defects, created at Motorola in the 1980s. Named after the statistical symbol for standard deviation.
A method for removing waste and delay from a process so that value flows to the customer faster. Developed from the Toyota Production System.
The five phases of a Lean Six Sigma project: Define, Measure, Analyse, Improve, Control. Each ends with a tollgate review before the next begins.
Read "Y is a function of x." The result you care about (Y) is caused by the inputs and process factors (x). To change a result, find and change its causes.
aliases: Y is a function of x

definition: A person trained to lead smaller improvement projects in their own area, usually part-time alongside a normal job.
A full-time improvement specialist who leads complex, cross-functional projects and mentors Green Belts.
An expert who trains and coaches Black and Green Belts and manages the improvement programme across an organisation.
The senior manager who sponsors a project: owns the business problem, selects the project, removes obstacles and approves tollgates. Also called the sponsor.
Basic awareness level. Team members who help collect data and take part in improvement events.
What the people who receive a process output need, expect and complain about. The source of requirements and defect definitions.
What the organisation needs from a process: cost, margin, compliance, growth. Sets why a project is worth doing.
What the people doing the work know about frustrations, workarounds and obstacles. Often the quickest route to real causes.
The habit of treating every process as something that can always be made better, in small steps, using data. Lean and Six Sigma are both forms of it.

The Greek letter σ, used in statistics for the standard deviation of a population. A "sigma level" describes how many standard deviations fit between the process average and the nearest customer limit.
A number describing how spread out a set of values is. Small means the values sit close together; large means they are scattered. Calculated on Day 7.
A concrete output a DMAIC phase must produce before its tollgate, such as a charter (Define) or a control plan (Control).
The review meeting at the end of each DMAIC phase where the sponsor checks the deliverables and approves moving to the next phase.
The manager responsible for a process day to day. Receives the improved process at the end of Control and keeps it running.
What a process produces for its customer. The output measure is the Y in Y = f(x).
Anything a process consumes or acts on: materials, information, requests, people's time. Inputs are among the x's in Y = f(x).
A unit of output that has one or more defects. A unit with three defects is one defective.
A capability index that compares the distance from the process mean to the nearest specification limit with three standard deviations. Falls when the process is off-centre.
Potential capability: the specification width divided by six standard deviations. Ignores where the process is centred.
The customer's boundary for acceptable output. The upper specification limit (USL) and lower specification limit (LSL) define the tolerance.
The parts of the work that change the product or service into something the customer wants and would pay for. Lean defines value from the customer's point of view, never the organisation's.
An activity that the customer would pay for, that transforms the item or moves the service forward, and that is done right first time. All three tests must be met.

Any activity that fails the value-added test. Some non-value-added work is still required (a legal check, a safety inspection); this is called business non-value-added and is minimised rather than removed.
The full sequence of steps, across departments, that delivers a product or service to a customer. Mapping it shows where value is added and where waste sits.
Arranging process steps so that an item moves through them without stopping, waiting or going backwards. The opposite of piling work up between steps.
Doing work only when the next step, and ultimately the customer, asks for it, so that production matches actual demand. Just-in-time is pull in practice.
Producing to a forecast or schedule and sending work on whether or not the next step is ready. Push creates piles of inventory between steps.
Any activity that consumes time, money or effort without adding value for the customer. The Japanese word is muda. Lean groups waste into seven kinds.
The manufacturing approach developed at Toyota from the 1950s by Taiichi Ohno and Shigeo Shingo, built on just-in-time and jidoka. Lean is the Western name for it.
Making and delivering only what is needed, when it is needed, in the amount needed. One of the two pillars of the Toyota Production System.

Building quality in by giving machines and people the ability to stop the process the moment a defect appears, so the problem is fixed at its source. The second pillar of the Toyota Production System, sometimes translated as automation with a human touch.
Continuous small improvements made by the people who do the work. A kaizen event is a short focused workshop, usually a few days, that improves one process area.
The seven kinds of waste identified by Taiichi Ohno: transport, inventory, motion, waiting, overproduction, over-processing and defects. Remembered with the mnemonic TIMWOOD.
The waste of moving the product, materials or documents between locations. It is movement of the thing being worked on; movement of people is motion.
The waste of anything held that is not being worked on right now: raw material, finished goods, work in process, or a backlog of unprocessed information such as unread emails.
The waste of people moving without adding value: walking, reaching, searching, switching between screens. Movement of the item itself is transport.
The waste of idle time when an item or a person waits for the next step, an approval, a machine or information.
The waste of making more than is needed or making it earlier than needed. Ohno called it the worst waste because it creates the other six.
The waste of doing more work on an item than the customer requires: extra approvals, unnecessary precision, re-entering the same data, adding features nobody asked for.

A Lean method for organising a workplace in five steps: Sort, Straighten, Shine, Standardise, Self-discipline. It makes waste visible and stops it recurring. Straighten is also called Set in Order and Self-discipline is also called Sustain.
Items that have entered a process but not yet left it: partly finished work waiting between steps. A form of inventory.
A group of items collected and processed together at each step. Batching makes every item wait for the whole group; reducing batch size shortens lead time without extra cost.
Arranging the workplace so that anyone can see at a glance whether things are normal or abnormal: marked shelves, colour codes, boards showing status. 5S is its foundation.
The actual place where the work happens. Going to gemba means observing a process first hand instead of reading about it in a report.
The ordinary, ever-present scatter built into a process from many small sources. It is predictable within a stable band and can only be reduced by changing the process itself.

Variation from something unusual that is not normally part of the process, such as a machine fault or an untrained operator. It shows up as an unexpected result or pattern and is removed by finding the specific cause.
One item of process output: one invoice, one patient discharge, one pump. Defects per unit and yield are counted per unit.
One distinct, pre-defined chance for a unit to be wrong. An invoice with five fields that can be wrong has five opportunities. Total opportunities equals units multiplied by opportunities per unit.
Defects per unit: total defects divided by total units inspected. It can be greater than 1 because a unit may carry several defects.
Defects per opportunity: total defects divided by total opportunities (units × opportunities per unit). A proportion between 0 and 1.
Defects per million opportunities: DPO multiplied by 1 000 000. The standard scale for comparing processes and the input to the sigma table.
The proportion of units that come out right. First time yield excludes units that needed rework; final yield, measured after rework, hides the cost of fixing things.
For one process step, the number of units that pass without any rework or scrap divided by the number that entered. Units repaired and then passed do not count.
The first time yields of every step in a process multiplied together: the probability that a unit passes through the whole process without a single defect. Always lower than the worst single step.
The time a process takes to complete one unit, from when work starts on that unit to when it is finished.
The total elapsed time from the customer's request to delivery, including all waiting. Lead time is what the customer feels; cycle time is what the process is doing.
A single number describing how many defects a process makes, read from DPMO using the standard sigma table. Higher is better; 6 sigma is 3.4 DPMO with the 1.5-sigma shift included.

The convention, from Motorola, that a process measured over a short period drifts by about 1.5 standard deviations in the long run. The standard sigma table adds 1.5 to the value the normal distribution would give, so 3.4 DPMO is called 6 sigma rather than 4.5.
The total cost an organisation incurs because its output is not right first time. Sorted into four categories: internal failure, external failure, appraisal and prevention.
The cost of defects found before the output reaches the customer: scrap, rework, re-testing, downtime, sorting.
The cost of defects found after delivery to the customer: warranty claims, returns, refunds, complaint handling, penalties, recalls and lost customers. The most expensive category per defect.
The cost of checking and inspecting to find defects: inspection, testing, audits, calibration, document review. Incurred whether or not defects are found.
The cost of stopping defects from happening: training, mistake-proofing, process design, supplier qualification. The cheapest way to spend a quality dollar.
The unofficial rework and checking that exists only to fix the output of the official process. Most of its cost never appears in the accounts.
Ranking categories of a problem from largest to smallest to find the few that produce most of the effect. Based on the 80:20 rule and applied to quality by Joseph Juran.
The observation that roughly 80% of an effect comes from roughly 20% of the causes. The split is rarely exactly 80:20; the point is that a few categories dominate.
The small number of categories that produce most of a problem, as opposed to the trivial many (also called the useful many). Juran's terms.
A bar chart of categories sorted from the largest count to the smallest, with a line showing the cumulative percentage. The tall bars on the left are the vital few.
Work done to fix a defective unit so that it passes. An internal failure cost, and part of the hidden factory.
Output that is thrown away because it cannot be fixed economically. An internal failure cost.
Whoever receives the output of a process. Customers can be external (outside the organisation) or internal (the next process or department).

A person or team inside the organisation that receives the output of a process. Payroll is the internal customer of the timesheet process. Internal customers have requirements and can receive defects.
A person or organisation outside the business that pays for or uses its output.
Something the customer needs the output to be or do, whether stated or assumed. Requirements come from the customer, not from what the organisation finds convenient to promise.
A customer need translated into a measurable characteristic of the output, with a measure, a target and a specification limit. The CTQ is the project's Y.
A three-level diagram that drills from a customer need to its drivers to measurable critical to quality characteristics.
A way of sorting customer needs into basic needs (expected, anger if missing), performance needs (more is better) and delighters (unexpected, pleasing). Developed by Noriaki Kano.
A written description of exactly how a measure is taken (what counts, which clock, which record) so that two people measuring the same thing get the same answer.
The first step (the trigger) and the last step (the handover of the output) that define where a process starts and ends. Boundaries set the scope of a project.

The one- or two-page document that authorises a project: business case, problem statement, goal statement, scope, team and timeline. Signed by the Champion, it is the main Define deliverable and is revisited at every tollgate.
A short statement of what is wrong, where, since when, how much (a measured Y) and with what impact. It must not name a cause or a solution.
A statement of what the primary metric will be by when, written in the same measure as the problem statement and tested against SMART. It must not describe the solution.
The part of the charter that says which process, boundaries, sites, products and customers are inside the project and which are out. Scope creep is a boundary problem fixed with the Champion.
The short argument for why the organisation should fund a project: what the problem costs now, what the improvement is worth, how it supports strategy and what happens if nothing is done.
A planned date for a significant point in the project, usually each DMAIC tollgate. The charter's timeline is a list of milestones.
Anyone with an interest in the process or the project who can help or block it, including people outside the team. Charters often list stakeholders and how each will be kept informed.
A goal that is Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound. The test applied to a goal statement.
A tool for grouping many written statements (for example customer comments on cards) into a small number of themes so that they can be turned into needs.

A five-column high-level diagram of a process: Suppliers, Inputs, Process (five to seven steps), Outputs, Customers. Built from the Process column outwards and used in Define to agree the process and its boundaries.
Anyone or anything that provides an input to a process: an outside company, another department, a computer system or the customer themselves.
The single measure of the Y that the problem statement and goal statement are written in and that the project will baseline, improve and track. One per project.

A process measure (an x) or related output that the team expects to move with the primary metric and that helps explain why it moved. Distinct from the consequential metrics that guard against side effects.
The value of a metric before the improvement, measured over a period long enough to capture normal variation, typically three to twelve months of historical data. Confirmed in Measure.
The value of the primary metric that the goal statement commits to. The gap between baseline and target, converted to money, is the project's benefit.
A saving that appears in the profit and loss account and can be audited: lower spending, more revenue or cash released. Fewer credit notes, less overtime, freed inventory.
A real benefit that does not appear directly as money: staff time freed but not removed, better customer satisfaction, lower risk, improved morale, and usually cost avoidance.
Spending that would have been needed but now is not, such as a planned extra shift no longer required. Usually treated as a soft benefit unless a budgeted cost is cancelled.
The time until a project's saving repays its one-off cost: cost divided by saving per period, expressed in that period's units.
(Benefit − cost) ÷ cost, expressed as a percentage, usually over one year. Measures how much a project earns relative to what it cost.

The sum of a project's future cash flows, each discounted for the years until it arrives, minus the up-front cost. A positive value means the project earns more than the organisation's required rate. Finance calculates it; Green Belts interpret it.

Making sure the savings promised in the charter actually arrive: a finance representative validates the method and the result, benefits are measured against the baseline for an agreed period after handover, and are net of costs.
The member of the finance team assigned to a project who validates the baseline cost, agrees the calculation method and signs off the realised saving. Decides what counts as a hard benefit.
Choosing which candidate projects to run by scoring them on benefit, strategic fit, probability of success, resources needed and data availability, often with a weighted scoring matrix.
A project cost paid once, such as training, a software change or a new fixture. Kept separate from recurring savings when calculating payback.
A saving that repeats every period after the improvement, such as fewer credit notes each month. Multiplied by twelve to give the annual saving.

A measure watched to make sure an improvement does not cause harm elsewhere, such as cycle time on a project that reduces errors. Also called a guard-rail metric. It must not get worse while the primary metric improves.
The International Association for Six Sigma Certification, the body that sets the Green Belt exam this course prepares for and publishes the Body of Knowledge the course follows.
aliases: International Association for Six Sigma Certification

definition: A document that cancels part or all of an invoice so the customer pays less. Issuing one because an invoice was wrong is an external failure cost.
Recorded observations: numbers, categories or counts written down according to a rule. Every statistic in the course is calculated from data.

Data measured on a scale that can be divided as finely as the instrument allows: time, weight, length, temperature, cost. Between any two values another value is possible. Carries more information per observation than discrete data.
Data that take only separate values with nothing in between, from counting or classifying. Includes attribute data (categories) and count data (whole numbers).
Discrete data that classify each unit into a category: pass/fail, late/on time, defective/not. Many units together give a proportion. Needs large samples.
Discrete data recording how many events occurred in a unit or period: defects per invoice, complaints per week. Always a whole number.
Every unit you want to draw a conclusion about, such as all invoices raised this year. Described by parameters (μ, σ). Usually too large or impossible to measure in full, so a sample is taken.
The subset of a population that is actually measured. Its statistics (x̄, s) estimate the population's parameters. Its value depends entirely on how representative it is.
A number that describes a whole population, written with a Greek letter: μ (mu) for the mean, σ (sigma) for the standard deviation.
A number calculated from a sample, written with a Roman letter: x̄ (x bar) for the sample mean, s for the sample standard deviation. Used to estimate the corresponding parameter.

Selecting units so that every unit in the population has an equal chance of being chosen, using a chance mechanism such as random numbers. The unbiased reference method; needs a list of the population.
Dividing the population into groups (strata) expected to differ, such as shifts or sites, then sampling randomly within each group. Guarantees every group is represented and lets groups be compared.
Taking every k-th unit after a random start, for example every 20th invoice. Easy to run in a live process; fails when the process has a cycle that matches the interval (periodicity).
Taking whatever units are easiest to reach, such as the top of the pile or Monday morning's calls. Not a valid method: whatever made them convenient usually makes them unrepresentative.
A systematic difference between the sample and the population caused by how the sample was selected. A larger sample does not remove it; only a better selection method does.
The number of units measured, written n. Precision improves with the square root of n. Discrete data need far larger samples than continuous data.

The Measure document that says for each measure what will be measured (with its operational definition), the data type, where and how often it is captured, the sampling method and size, who collects it and how it is recorded.

A simple form with tick boxes or tally marks for recording each occurrence as it happens, designed so the data can be used without re-typing. Recording conditions (shift, machine, operator) alongside the tally allows later stratification.
A comparison of a characteristic against a standard scale or reference, producing a recorded value. The measurement system that makes it is checked on Day 10 before its data are trusted.
Any characteristic that changes from unit to unit and can be measured or classified. The x's and the Y are all variables. Not to be confused with variable (continuous) data.
Numbers that summarise a data set: measures of the middle (mean, median, mode) and of spread (range, variance, standard deviation, interquartile range).
The ordinary average: the sum of the values divided by how many there are. Written x̄ for a sample, μ for a population. Uses every value, so it is pulled by outliers and skew.
The middle value of the sorted data (halfway between the two middle values if there is an even number). Half the values lie below it. Unaffected by outliers, so preferred for skewed data.
The value that occurs most often. The only measure of the middle that works for category data. A data set can have no mode or several.
The largest value minus the smallest. A quick measure of spread that uses only two values and grows with sample size.

The average squared distance of the values from their mean. In squared units. The sample variance s² divides by n − 1; the population variance σ² divides by N. Its square root is the standard deviation.
The square root of the sample variance: the sum of squared deviations from the mean divided by n − 1, then square-rooted. Written s. Used whenever the data are a sample, which is nearly always.
The square root of the population variance, dividing the sum of squared deviations by N (not N − 1). Written σ. Used only when every unit in the population has been measured.
One of the three values that split sorted data into four equal parts: Q1 (25% below), Q2 (the median) and Q3 (75% below). By hand, Q1 and Q3 are the medians of the lower and upper halves.
Q3 − Q1: the spread of the middle half of the data. Not affected by extremes. Values more than 1.5 × IQR beyond the quartiles are flagged as outliers.
A value so far from the rest of the data that it deserves investigation, conventionally beyond Q1 − 1.5 × IQR or Q3 + 1.5 × IQR. A signal to check the record, not an automatic deletion.

Asymmetry in a distribution: a long tail on one side. Right (positive) skew has the tail towards high values and the mean above the median; left skew the reverse. Times and costs are usually right-skewed.
Where the middle of a data set sits, described by the mean, median or mode.
How spread out the values in a data set are, described by the range, variance, standard deviation or interquartile range. Another word for variation.
A bar chart of continuous data grouped into equal-width intervals (bins), showing the shape of the distribution: symmetric, skewed, bimodal or truncated. It hides the time order.
A picture of a data set as a box from Q1 to Q3 with a line at the median, whiskers to the last values within 1.5 × IQR, and outliers as separate points. Several side by side compare groups.
Individual values plotted in time order with a line at the median. Shows trends, cycles and shifts that a histogram hides. A control chart is a run chart with control limits added.

Each observation plotted as a point with one variable on the horizontal axis and another on the vertical. Shows whether two variables move together, in which direction and how tightly. The starting point for correlation and regression.
Each value shown as a dot on a number line, stacked where values repeat. Like a histogram but keeps every value visible, so it suits small samples.
A distribution with two clear peaks. Usually means two different processes (shifts, machines, suppliers) have been mixed together and should be separated.
The standard deviation divided by the mean, as a percentage. Lets spread be compared between measures with different units or scales.
The symmetric bell-shaped distribution that many stable process measurements follow. Fully described by its mean and standard deviation. Assumed by capability indices, t-tests and ANOVA.
The everyday name for the shape of the normal distribution: a symmetric hump highest at the mean.
For a normal distribution, about 68% of values lie within 1 standard deviation of the mean, 95% within 2 and 99.7% within 3.

How many standard deviations a value sits above (positive) or below (negative) the mean: Z = (x − μ) ÷ σ. Strips away units so values from different processes can be compared and looked up in the Z table.
The normal distribution with mean 0 and standard deviation 1. Z-scores follow it, which is why one table serves every normal distribution.

A table giving, for each Z-score, the proportion of the standard normal distribution lying below it (the cumulative probability). For 'above', subtract from 1; for 'between', subtract two table values.
The proportion of a distribution lying at or below a given value. The Z table lists cumulative probabilities for the standard normal distribution.
A statistical test of whether data could have come from a normal distribution. The Anderson-Darling test is the usual one; a p-value below 0.05 means the data are not normal.
Sorted data plotted against the values a perfect normal distribution would give. Points close to a straight line mean the data are normal; curves at the ends mean skew or heavy tails.

The standard normality test. It reports a statistic (AD) and a p-value; p ≥ 0.05 means treat the data as normal, p < 0.05 means they are significantly non-normal. Oversensitive for very large samples.

The probability of seeing data at least as extreme as those observed if the null hypothesis were true. Compared with alpha (usually 0.05): below alpha is significant. For a normality test, a low p-value means the data are not normal. Explained fully on Day 14.
The thin end of a distribution, far from the mean. The normal distribution has two tails; 'one-tailed' and 'two-tailed' describe which tails a test or probability looks at.
A value below which a given percentage of the data falls. The 95th percentile of a normal distribution is the mean plus 1.645 standard deviations.
A diagram of the steps of a process in order, with decisions, loops and handoffs drawn using standard flowchart symbols. Drawn at increasing detail: SIPOC, high-level, detailed, swimlane.
Another name for a process map. Symbols: rounded box for start and end, rectangle for a step, diamond for a decision, parallelogram for input or output, triangle for a queue or inventory.

A detailed process map with a horizontal band (lane) for each department, role or system, so that every handoff is a line crossing lanes. Used to show who does what and where the delays between functions sit.
The process as it actually runs today, including workarounds and rework loops, as observed at gemba. Contrasted with the documented should-be process. Measure maps the as-is version.

A Lean map of the whole value stream from order to delivery showing process boxes with data, inventory between steps, information flow, and a timeline of waiting and processing time. Produces lead time, process time and process cycle efficiency.
The hands-on time to complete one unit at a step, excluding waiting. Also called touch time; on a value stream map it is the lower line of the timeline. Cycle time is used the same way.
Value-added time divided by lead time, as a percentage. Shows how much of the customer's wait is actual work. Unimproved processes typically run at 1% to 10%.
Available working time divided by customer demand: the time available to produce one unit if the process is to keep pace with the customer. Set by the customer, not the process.

Lead time = work in process ÷ throughput. The average time a unit spends in a process equals the number of units in it divided by the rate at which they leave. Cutting work in process cuts lead time directly.
The number of units a process completes per period, such as orders per day. Limited by the bottleneck.
The step whose capacity limits the throughput of the whole process; on a value stream map, a step whose process time per unit exceeds takt time. Queues build in front of it.
The time to switch a step or machine from making one product to making another. Recorded in the data box on a value stream map; long changeovers push processes towards large batches.
A floor plan with a line traced for every movement of a person or item during a process. A tangle of lines makes motion and transport waste visible.
The line along the bottom of a value stream map that alternates waiting time and process time for each step and totals both to give lead time and process time.
The value stream map of the process as it runs today, drawn in Measure. The baseline that the future state map is compared against.
The value stream map of the redesigned process with waste removed, drawn in Improve.

The set of studies (bias, linearity, stability, gage R&R, attribute agreement) that check whether a measurement system is accurate and precise enough for its data to be trusted. Done in Measure before the baseline and capability.
Everything involved in producing a measurement: the instrument, the person, the procedure, the environment and the recording. Its variation adds to the process variation in any data set.
Any measuring instrument: micrometer, scale, stopwatch, thermometer, a software timestamp. Also spelt gauge.
How closely repeated measurements of the same thing agree with each other, regardless of whether they are centred on the true value. Studied with gage R&R.
Whether measurements are centred on the true value: on average, the gauge reads what the item really is. Its components are bias, linearity and stability. Fixed by calibration.
The difference between the average of repeated measurements and the reference (true) value. A constant offset, expressed as a percentage of tolerance and corrected by calibration.
Whether the bias of a gauge stays the same across its operating range. Checked by measuring reference parts across the range and plotting bias against reference value.

Whether the bias of a gauge stays the same over time, checked by measuring the same reference part repeatedly over days and plotting the results. Drift means recalibration is needed. (For a process, stability means only common cause variation is present; Day 11.)
The smallest difference a gauge can display. Should be at least one-tenth of the tolerance or of the process variation being studied. Also called discrimination.

A study of a measurement system's precision, separating repeatability (equipment) from reproducibility (appraisers) and comparing their combined variation with the total variation and with the tolerance. Standard design: 10 parts, 3 appraisers, 2–3 repeats.
Variation when the same person measures the same part with the same gauge several times. The instrument's own noise, also called equipment variation (EV).
Variation between different people (appraisers) measuring the same parts with the same gauge. Comes from technique, also called appraiser variation (AV). Fixed by standard method and training.
The real differences between the parts in a gage R&R study, written PV. The variation the gauge is supposed to detect.
In a gage R&R study, the combination of measurement system variation and part-to-part variation: TV = √(GRR² + PV²).
Another name for repeatability: the standard deviation of repeated measurements by one person with one gauge. Written EV.
Another name for reproducibility: the variation between different people using the same gauge. Written AV.
GRR ÷ total variation × 100: the share of the observed spread that is measurement noise. Under 10% acceptable, 10–30% marginal, over 30% unacceptable.
6 × GRR ÷ (USL − LSL) × 100: the share of the customer's tolerance consumed by measurement noise. Under 10% acceptable, 10–30% marginal, over 30% unacceptable. Some older texts use 5.15 instead of 6.
1.41 × PV ÷ GRR, rounded down: how many separate groups the gauge can reliably sort the process output into. Must be at least 5.

The MSA for pass/fail or category judgements: several appraisers assess 30–50 known items twice each, and agreement within appraiser, between appraisers and with the known standard is reported, with kappa.

A statistic for attribute agreement that corrects the agreement rate for agreement expected by chance. Runs from −1 to 1; above 0.9 excellent, 0.7–0.9 acceptable, below 0.7 the measurement system needs work.
The accepted true value of a part or standard, established with a much better instrument or a certified reference, against which bias, linearity and stability are measured.
Adjusting a gauge against a reference value so that its bias is removed. Cures accuracy problems, not precision problems.
A person taking measurements or making judgements in a measurement system study. Differences between appraisers are reproducibility.
(GRR ÷ TV)² × 100: the measurement system's share of total variance (not standard deviation). Under 1% acceptable, 1–9% marginal, over 9% unacceptable.
The width between the customer's upper and lower specification limits: USL − LSL. Several measurement system results (bias, percent tolerance) and the capability index Cp are judged against it.
The comparison of what a process produces (its centre and spread) with what the customer specified (the specification limits). Summarised by a capability index and an expected defect rate.
A single number comparing process spread and centring with the specification: Cp, Cpk, Cpu, Cpl (short-term) or Pp, Ppk (long-term).
Capability against the upper specification limit only: (USL − mean) ÷ (3σ). Used alone when there is no lower limit.
Capability against the lower specification limit only: (mean − LSL) ÷ (3σ). Used alone when there is no upper limit.
Long-term potential capability: (USL − LSL) ÷ (6 × overall standard deviation). The long-term equivalent of Cp.
Long-term capability using the overall standard deviation and the nearest specification limit. Describes what the customer actually received over the period; usually lower than Cpk.
The variation within rational subgroups of consecutive units made under the same conditions. Excludes shifts and drifts between subgroups. The basis of Cp and Cpk; written σ within.
The variation of all data taken together over a long period, including every shift and drift. The ordinary standard deviation of everything collected; the basis of Pp and Ppk; written σ overall.
Another name for short-term variation: the spread inside rational subgroups, estimated from the average range or standard deviation of the subgroups.
Another name for long-term variation: the standard deviation of the whole data set.

A process showing only common cause variation, so that its mean and spread are predictable and tomorrow looks like today. Confirmed with a control chart. Capability indices are meaningful only for a stable process.

A limit calculated from the process's own data (typically the mean ± 3 standard deviations of the plotted statistic) that shows what the process is doing. The voice of the process; never a specification limit.

The ordered procedure for measuring capability: verify the gauge, collect rational subgroups over time, confirm stability, check normality, then calculate Cp/Cpk and Pp/Ppk and the expected defect rate.
How close the process mean sits to the middle of the specification. Measured by the gap between Cp and Cpk: a large gap means the process is off-centre.
A small group of consecutive units collected under the same conditions so that only common cause variation can occur inside it. The basis of short-term variation and of control charts.
Capability stated for pass/fail or count data: DPMO, yield and sigma level from the sigma table, rather than Cp and Cpk.
Another name for attribute capability: capability for counted or classified data.

The single Z whose one-tailed area equals the total expected proportion outside both specification limits. Software reports Z bench within (short-term) and overall (long-term); the difference is the process's actual shift.
The published table converting DPMO to sigma level. It reports short-term sigma by adding the 1.5 shift to the Z the normal distribution gives for that DPMO.

Keeping capability current after a project: a running control chart, periodic recalculation of Cpk or DPMO plotted over time, re-verification of the gauge, and the figures recorded in the control plan.
What a process delivers over months, including drift and shifts: Pp/Ppk, Z bench overall, or DPMO measured over a long period.
What a process can do within a subgroup under one set of conditions, its potential: Cp/Cpk, Z bench within, or the sigma level read from the sigma table.
Parts per million: the expected number of units (or measurements) outside specification per million produced. Software reports expected PPM within and overall on a capability report.

A diagram with the problem (effect) at the head and categories of possible causes on the bones, filled by brainstorming. Also called the Ishikawa or fishbone diagram. It lists possibilities; it proves nothing.
The common name for the cause-and-effect diagram, from its shape: a spine to the effect with main bones for each category of cause.
The standard fishbone categories: Man (people), Machine, Material, Method, Measurement, Mother Nature (environment). Service processes often use the 4P set: Policies, Procedures, People, Plant.
A structured group session for listing ideas without judging them: define the problem first, everyone contributes, quantity before quality, write everything down.
Asking "why does that happen?" repeatedly, typically about five times, to move from a symptom to an actionable root cause.
A cause which, if removed, stops the effect recurring, as opposed to a symptom that returns. Declared only after data confirm it.
IASSC's name for the cause-and-effect matrix: a table scoring candidate x's against weighted customer outputs to rank the x's for further study.
A table with weighted outputs (Y's) across the top and candidate inputs (x's) down the side. Each cell is scored 0, 1, 3 or 9 for the strength of the relationship; row totals rank the x's.

Failure modes and effects analysis: for each step or input, list how it could fail, the effect, and score severity, occurrence and detection to give a risk priority number, then assign actions. Used to rank x's by risk and to check new designs.
A specific way a step or input could go wrong, such as "purchase order number missing". One step can have several.
In an FMEA, what the customer or the next step experiences when a failure mode occurs. Severity is scored on the effect.
FMEA score, 1 to 10, for how serious the effect of a failure is. Changed only by redesign, not by inspection or reduced frequency.
FMEA score, 1 to 10, for how often the cause produces the failure. Reduced by prevention. Based on defect-rate data where available.
FMEA score, 1 to 10, for how likely current controls are to catch the failure before it reaches the customer. The scale runs backwards: 1 means almost certain detection, 10 means none.
Severity × occurrence × detection in an FMEA, from 1 to 1 000. Higher means higher priority for action, but a high severity deserves action even at a modest RPN.
In an FMEA, the measures already in place to prevent a cause or detect a failure before it reaches the customer. They determine the detection score.
The FMEA column recording what will be done to reduce a risk, with owner and date, followed by the revised severity, occurrence, detection and RPN once done.
The short list of candidate causes, ranked by the X-Y matrix and FMEA, that Analyse will test with data. Distinct from the vital few categories of a Pareto chart.
Drawing conclusions about a population from a sample, with a statement of how sure you can be. Confidence intervals and hypothesis tests are inference.
A sample statistic used as the best guess of a population parameter. It is never exact; the standard error and confidence interval say how far off it might be.
The distribution that a statistic (such as the sample mean) would have over many repeated samples of the same size. The central limit theorem describes it for the mean.
The standard deviation of a sample statistic over repeated samples. For the mean, σ ÷ √n (or s ÷ √n). It shrinks with the square root of the sample size.

For samples of reasonable size (about 30 or more), the distribution of sample means is approximately normal with mean μ and standard deviation σ ÷ √n, whatever the shape of the population. It is about averages, not individual values.
A range of population values consistent with the sample: estimate ± critical value × standard error. A 95% interval is produced by a method that captures the true value 95% of the time.
The long-run capture rate chosen for a confidence interval, usually 95%. Higher levels give wider intervals.
The half-width of a confidence interval: critical value × standard error.
A formal procedure for deciding whether an effect seen in a sample is real or could be chance: state H₀ and H₁, choose alpha, compute a test statistic and p-value, and reject or fail to reject H₀.
H₀: the statement of no effect, no difference or no change that a hypothesis test assumes true until the data make it implausible. It is rejected or not rejected; it is never accepted.
H₁ (or Hₐ): the claim the test is trying to demonstrate, such as "the means differ" (two-tailed) or "the new rate is lower" (one-tailed).
The significance level: the largest p-value at which H₀ will be rejected, usually 0.05. Equal to the probability of a Type I error.
The probability of a Type II error: failing to reject H₀ when it is false. Power is 1 − beta.
Rejecting a true null hypothesis: concluding there is an effect when there is none (a false alarm). Its probability is alpha. Also called producer's risk.
Failing to reject a false null hypothesis: missing an effect that is real. Its probability is beta. Also called consumer's risk.
The probability that a test detects an effect that is really there: 1 − beta. Rises with sample size, effect size and alpha. A common target is 0.80.
The number a hypothesis test calculates from the data (a Z, t, F or chi-square value) to compare with a critical value or convert to a p-value.
The table value of a test statistic at the chosen alpha; the null hypothesis is rejected when the test statistic is beyond it. Equivalent to comparing the p-value with alpha.
A result with a p-value at or below alpha, meaning it is unlikely to be chance. Says nothing about whether the effect is large enough to matter.
Whether an effect is big enough to matter to the customer or the business, judged from the effect size and the business case, independently of the p-value.

A test whose alternative hypothesis states a direction (greater than, or less than). All of alpha sits in one tail, so the critical Z at 5% is 1.645. The direction must be chosen before seeing the data.
A test whose alternative hypothesis is "not equal", so alpha is split between both tails; the critical Z at 5% is 1.96. Used when a difference in either direction matters.
A test comparing one sample with a fixed target value, such as whether the mean fill weight is 250 g.
A test comparing two independent samples with each other, such as whether two shifts differ. A paired test instead compares two measurements on the same units.
Roughly the number of independent pieces of information behind an estimate; determines which row of a t, F or chi-square table to use. For a one-sample mean it is n − 1.
The actual size of a difference or relationship (for example a 2-minute difference in means), reported alongside the p-value so practical significance can be judged.
A hypothesis test for a mean (or a difference between means) that uses the t distribution because the standard deviation is estimated from the sample. Comes in 1-sample, 2-sample and paired forms.
A bell-shaped distribution slightly wider than the normal, used when the standard deviation is estimated from the sample. Its width depends on the degrees of freedom; by about 30 it is almost normal.
Tests whether a population mean equals a target value: t = (x̄ − μ₀) ÷ (s ÷ √n), df = n − 1.
Tests whether two independent populations have the same mean, using the difference between sample means divided by its standard error. Pooled and Welch versions exist.
Tests whether the mean difference between two measurements on the same units is zero: a 1-sample t-test on the differences, df = number of pairs − 1.
The 2-sample t-test that assumes equal variances, averaging the two sample variances into one pooled estimate; df = n₁ + n₂ − 2.
The 2-sample t-test that does not assume equal variances; each variance is used separately and the degrees of freedom are reduced by a formula. The safer default.

The assumption, needed by the pooled t-test and by ANOVA, that the groups being compared have similar spread. Checked with an F-test, Levene's test, or the rule that the largest standard deviation is under twice the smallest.
Tests whether a population variance equals a hypothesised value: χ² = (n − 1)s² ÷ σ₀², df = n − 1, compared with the chi-square distribution. Sensitive to non-normality.
A right-skewed distribution starting at zero, written χ², used for tests of a variance and for chi-square tests on counts. Its two-tailed critical values differ at each end.
Compares two variances by their ratio F = s₁² ÷ s₂² (larger over smaller). Used to decide between the pooled and Welch t-tests; Levene's test is a less normality-sensitive alternative.
A condition a statistical test's mathematics relies on, such as normality, equal variances or independence. When an assumption fails the p-value is not trustworthy.
The condition that one observation does not influence another. Required by every test in the course; usually secured by sampling design and random order of collection.

Analysis of variance: a test of whether three or more group means are equal, done by comparing between-group variation with within-group variation through the F statistic. Uses one alpha for all groups at once.
ANOVA with a single factor (one categorical x with several levels) and a continuous Y. H₀: all group means equal; H₁: at least one differs.
A categorical x in ANOVA, such as supplier or shift, whose categories are called levels.
One category of a factor: the day shift is one level of the factor shift.
The ratio of between-group mean square to within-group mean square in ANOVA. About 1 when the group means are equal; large when they differ.
The right-skewed distribution of the F statistic, with two degrees of freedom (between and within). Used to find the p-value for ANOVA and the two-variance F-test.
A total of squared deviations. In ANOVA, SS total = SS between + SS within; each divided by its degrees of freedom gives a mean square.
How much the group means scatter around the overall mean in ANOVA. The factor row of the table. Larger than within-group variation when the groups really differ.
How much values scatter around their own group mean in ANOVA: the ordinary process noise. The error row of the table.
A sum of squares divided by its degrees of freedom: a variance. F = MS between ÷ MS within.
The standard layout of an ANOVA: rows for factor, error and total; columns for degrees of freedom, sum of squares, mean square, F and p. Degrees of freedom and sums of squares add down the column.
SS between ÷ SS total: the share of the variation in Y explained by the factor. Answers practical significance; a significant factor can still explain little.
A pairwise comparison run after a significant ANOVA to find which groups differ, using a method that controls the overall Type I risk, such as Tukey's test.

The standard post-hoc method: confidence intervals for every pairwise difference of means, adjusted so the overall alpha is held. Software shows grouping letters; groups sharing a letter do not differ.
An observed value minus the value a model predicts for it: in ANOVA, the value minus its group mean; in regression, the value minus the fitted line. Residuals are checked for normality and patterns.
The ANOVA assumption that all groups have similar spread. Checked with Levene's or Bartlett's test or the two-to-one standard deviation rule; Welch ANOVA is used when it fails.
Tests whether a population proportion equals a target: Z = (p̂ − p₀) ÷ √(p₀(1 − p₀) ÷ n). Valid when n·p₀ and n·(1 − p₀) are both at least 5; software otherwise uses an exact binomial method.
Tests whether two independent proportions are equal, using the pooled proportion in the standard error. Equivalent to a 2 × 2 chi-square test.
Tests whether two categorical variables in a contingency table are associated: χ² = Σ(O − E)² ÷ E with df = (rows − 1)(columns − 1). A significant result shows association, not causation.
A table of counts with one categorical variable in the rows and another in the columns. The input to the chi-square test of independence.
The count a contingency-table cell would have if the row and column variables were independent: row total × column total ÷ grand total. Each should be at least 5 for the chi-square test.
The actual count in a contingency-table cell, written O in the chi-square formula.

A relationship between two categorical variables: the distribution of one differs across the levels of the other. Shown by a significant chi-square test; it does not establish which cells differ or that one variable causes the other.
A chi-square test comparing one set of observed counts with the counts a claimed distribution predicts, df = categories − 1.
The combined proportion (x₁ + x₂) ÷ (n₁ + n₂) used in the standard error of the 2-proportion test under the null hypothesis that both groups share one proportion.
The rule that every cell's expected count in a chi-square test should be at least 5; sparse categories are combined or more data collected when it fails.

A hypothesis test that makes no assumption about the shape of the distribution, usually by working on the ranks of the data rather than the values. Used for non-normal continuous data with small samples; tests medians.
A test that assumes the data follow a particular distribution, usually the normal, and tests its parameter, usually the mean: t-tests and ANOVA.
A value's position when the data are sorted: 1 for the smallest, 2 for the next. Non-parametric tests replace values with ranks so that outliers cannot dominate.
The non-parametric equivalent of the 2-sample t-test: compares the medians of two independent groups by ranking all values together. Also called the Wilcoxon rank-sum test.

The non-parametric equivalent of one-way ANOVA: tests whether three or more independent groups have the same median. Its statistic H is compared with chi-square on k − 1 df; a significant result needs pairwise follow-up.

Compares medians of two or more groups by counting values above and below the overall median and running a chi-square test on the counts. Less powerful than Kruskal-Wallis but more robust to outliers.

The non-parametric test for three or more related conditions in a blocked design (each unit measured under every condition). Ranks within each block; the rank equivalent of a two-way ANOVA without interaction.

Tests whether a median equals a target by counting values above and below the target, ignoring their size, using the binomial distribution. Works for any data including ordinal, but has the least power.

Tests whether a median equals a target using the signs and the ranked sizes of the differences from the target. More powerful than the sign test; assumes the distribution is symmetric. Also used for paired differences.
Describes a method whose result changes little when an assumption is violated or an outlier is present. Non-parametric tests and the median are robust; the mean and t-tests are less so.

A study in which each unit (block), such as an operator or a machine, is measured under every condition, so that differences between units can be removed from the comparison. Analysed with a paired test (two conditions) or Friedman (three or more).
The decision table that maps data type (continuous or attribute), number and independence of groups, and normality to the correct hypothesis test.

A passive graphical study that samples a running process at several positions, consecutive units and times, and plots the results to show which family of variation (positional, cyclical or temporal) dominates, so the search for x's can be narrowed.
The plot of a multi-vari study: time along the horizontal axis, clusters of consecutive units at each time, and the positions within each unit joined by a vertical line.

Variation across positions within one unit or batch: cavities of a mould, positions on a sheet, fields on a form. Points to spatial causes such as tooling or fixtures. Also called within-piece variation.
Variation between consecutive units or batches made under the same conditions. Points to causes acting on each unit, such as material lot or technique. Also called piece-to-piece variation.
Variation across longer periods: hour to hour, shift to shift, day to day. Points to causes that change with time, such as warm-up, wear or shift changeover. Also called time-to-time variation.
Another name for positional variation.
Another name for cyclical variation.
Another name for temporal variation.

The pattern of values a variable takes and how often each occurs. The class of distribution (normal, exponential, Poisson, binomial, Weibull) decides which capability method, control chart and test apply.
A right-skewed continuous distribution for the time between random independent events occurring at a constant rate λ. Mean 1 ÷ λ (the mean time between failures); median below the mean.

A discrete distribution for the count of events in a fixed interval when events occur independently at a constant average rate λ: defects per unit, calls per hour. Mean and variance both equal λ. P(0) = e^(−λ).
A discrete distribution for the number of successes in n independent trials each with probability p: defective units in a sample of 50. Mean n·p, standard deviation √(n·p·(1 − p)).
A flexible continuous distribution for time to failure. Its shape parameter β describes the failure rate: below 1 early-life failures, 1 constant (the exponential), above 1 wear-out.
A distribution of a variable that takes only whole-number values: Poisson and binomial.
A distribution of a variable that can take any value in a range: normal, exponential and Weibull.
The average time between failures of equipment; for a constant failure rate it is the mean of an exponential distribution, 1 ÷ λ.
The degree to which two continuous variables move together in a straight-line relationship, measured by Pearson's r from −1 to +1. Correlation is association, not causation.
r: a number from −1 to +1 whose sign gives the direction and whose size gives the strength of the linear relationship between two variables. Unitless; measures straight-line association only.
r², the square of the correlation: the proportion of the variation in Y explained by its linear relationship with x. Reported by software as R-Sq.
x causing Y. A correlation is consistent with causation but also with reverse causation, a lurking variable or coincidence; only a controlled change to x (a pilot) demonstrates it.
A third variable that drives both x and Y and so creates a correlation between them without either causing the other. Also called a confounder.
Fitting a straight line Y = b₀ + b₁x through a scatter plot by least squares so that Y can be predicted from one x. "Simple" means one predictor.
The fitted line Y = b₀ + b₁x (or with more terms in multiple regression). b₀ is the intercept and b₁ the slope.
b₁ in the regression equation: the change in Y for each one-unit increase in x. Its p-value tests whether x has a linear effect on Y.
b₀ in the regression equation: the predicted Y when x = 0. Often outside the range of the data and then has no physical meaning.
The Y the regression line predicts at a given x, written ŷ. Observed Y minus fitted value is the residual.
The method that chooses the regression line minimising the sum of the squared residuals (vertical distances from the points to the line).

Checking a regression's assumptions by plotting the residuals: normal probability plot (straight = normal), residuals versus fitted values (random band = linear, funnel = unequal variance), histogram, and residuals versus order (no trend = independent).
S: the typical size of a residual, in Y's units. Predictions from the line are uncertain by roughly ±2S.
Predicting Y for an x outside the range of the data used to fit the line. Unsupported by the fit, since the relationship may change beyond the data.
The regression assumption that the true relationship between x and Y is a straight line. A curve in the residuals-versus-fitted plot shows it has failed.
Regression of Y on two or more predictors at once: Y = b₀ + b₁x₁ + b₂x₂ + …. Each coefficient is the effect of its x with the other predictors held constant.
R² corrected for the number of predictors: it rises only when a new predictor improves the fit by more than chance. Used to compare models with different numbers of terms.

Correlation among the predictors in a multiple regression, which inflates the standard errors of the coefficients and makes them unstable. Detected by VIF; fixed by removing or combining correlated predictors.
VIF: how much a coefficient's variance is inflated by correlation with the other predictors. 1 means none; above 5 is a concern and above 10 is serious.
Fitting a curve rather than a straight line, most often by adding a squared term (Y = b₀ + b₁x + b₂x²). Judged by adjusted R² and the residual plots.
An x² term added to a regression to fit a curve. A negative coefficient bends the curve downward (a peak); positive bends it upward.

term: confidence interval for the mean response
definition: The range in which the average Y of all units with a given x is likely to lie. Reflects only the uncertainty of the fitted line; narrower than the prediction interval.

The range in which a single new observation with a given x is likely to fall. Includes the line's uncertainty and the scatter of individual values, so it is always wider than the confidence interval for the mean.

Replacing a variable with a function of itself (log, square root, reciprocal) and analysing the transformed values, to make skewed data normal, straighten a curve or equalise variance. Limits must be transformed the same way.
A family of power transformations Y^λ from which software chooses the λ that makes the data most nearly normal. λ = 1 none, 0.5 square root, 0 log, −1 reciprocal. Needs positive data.
λ, the power in the Box-Cox transformation. Rounded to a plain value: 1 (no transformation), 0.5 (square root), 0 (logarithm), −1 (reciprocal).
Replacing right-skewed positive data (times, costs, counts) with their logarithms to pull in the long tail. The Box-Cox choice when λ is near 0.
An x variable in a regression. Also called an independent variable or regressor.
The Y variable in a regression: the output being predicted. Also called the dependent variable.
